turns.doctor_question: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, yeah, it's nice to meet you too. Um, I guess I'm here because... well, I’ve just been doing these things lately at work and at school that really just do not make any sense at all. I work as a bookkeeping clerk, right? So I deal with a lot of paperwork, mostly accounts payable, reconciling expenses, making sure the math adds up, that kind of thing. But lately, instead of just doing my job, I've been getting stuck doing this weird stuff. 

Like, the other day, I had this massive stack of expense reports, and I took all these receipts, and instead of entering them into the system, I just started lining them up across the floor. Just one by one, making this huge, perfectly straight line all the way across the office carpet, and I didn't even really know why I was doing it, but I spent like twenty minutes just aligning them. 

And then with my ten-key—my calculator, which I use all day for auditing—I can't just type the numbers in normally right now. I have started tapping the calculator in sets of nine. Like, I'll just sit there tapping the plastic casing or the clear button, exactly nine times. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine. Over and over before I can actually do any of the math. It’s so distracting and it takes up so much time. 

But I think the part that really freaked out my coworker, and the reason I finally made this appointment, is the copier. I’ll go over to the machine to scan the ledgers or whatever, and I’ll just stop. I’ll stand there by the copier with my hands held up in the air, almost like I'm waiting to catch a basketball or like I'm just totally frozen, and I will literally just stand there holding my hands up until someone walks by and asks if I am okay. And as soon as they ask, I just put my hands down and snap out of it like nothing happened. I just don't know why my body is doing these things, but it's really starting to get in the way of everything.

symptom_reasoning.S022: The patient describes bizarre, disorganized motor behaviors, including stereotyped tapping, purposeless arranging of receipts, and posturing (standing frozen with hands held up).

turns.doctor_question: When you feel the need to tap the calculator nine times, is it because a thought keeps bothering you until you do it?
turns.patient_response:
Well, no, actually, and I think that's the part that is so incredibly confusing about all of this. You'd think there would be some kind of reason or some specific worry, right? Like, I've seen movies or read things online where people feel like they have to flip a light switch or wash their hands because they have this terrifying thought that something awful is going to happen to their family if they don't. But for me, it is not like that at all. 

There isn't any nagging thought in my head telling me, you know, "hey, you have to tap this calculator exactly nine times or the company is going to go bankrupt" or "you're going to get fired." It's more like... my hand just does it. I'll just be sitting there at my desk, looking at a stack of invoices—like yesterday, it was these invoices from the main hardware supplier we use, and they always send these really messy, faded carbon copies that are just super hard to read—and I'll be getting ready to punch in the totals, and then my finger is just suddenly tapping the plastic casing. 

And my brain is honestly completely empty of any worry while it's happening. I'm not thinking about anything at all, really. It's just this physical rhythm that my hand decides to do all on its own, and I just sort of sit there and watch it happen until the nine taps are done. I don't feel anxious before I do it, and I don't feel this big sense of relief after I do it, either. Which honestly makes it even harder to explain to my boss or my coworkers when they walk by and I'm just tapping away at the side of the ten-key instead of actually adding up the columns. It’s just a completely empty, physical thing.

symptom_reasoning.S065: The patient explicitly denies having any nagging, intrusive thoughts or worries that prompt the tapping behavior.
symptom_reasoning.S066: The patient denies that the repetitive tapping is performed in response to an obsession or to prevent/relieve anxiety, stating it is just an empty physical action.

turns.doctor_question: Right before these movements happen, do you feel a buildup or urge in your body that you can hold back for a little while?

No tension in my muscles, no weird tingle in my fingers before I start tapping the ten-key, no... no pressure building up in my chest or my arms before I just freeze with my hands up at the copier.

Like, just yesterday, I was sitting at my desk, and I had this huge stack of reconciliation forms—the ones for the third quarter that are always a complete nightmare because the sales team literally never categorizes their travel expenses right, they just dump it all under miscellaneous—and I was just looking at my dual monitors, totally relaxed, just trying to figure out if a hotel receipt was supposed to be lodging or client entertainment, and then... boom. Next thing I know, my hand is just tapping the plastic. One, two, three, four... all the way to nine. 

I didn't feel anything right before it started. I couldn't have held it back because I didn't even know it was about to happen until it was already happening. It's just like someone flips a switch and my body just does the movement without asking my permission or giving me any kind of heads-up, you know? It's completely spontaneous. So, yeah, no buildup or urge at all. It's just... sudden.

Just one after the other, end to end. 

And then there's the tapping the calculator in sets of nine, over and over, before I can even start auditing a ledger. It's just... I don't know, it's like my body is just doing these completely random, nonsensical things—the receipts on the floor, the tapping, the freezing with my hands up until someone checks on me—and it's really starting to disrupt my life. I just want to understand why I'm doing things that have absolutely no logic to them.

symptom_reasoning.S022: The patient describes engaging in bizarre, nonsensical behaviors such as freezing with hands up, lining receipts across the floor, and tapping a calculator in sets of nine, which are indicative of disorganized or abnormal motor behavior.

turns.doctor_question: When these episodes happen, does it ever feel like an outside force is controlling your body?
turns.patient_response:
Um, no, not really like... I don't feel like a puppet on strings or anything. It's not like an invisible hand is grabbing my wrist and forcing me to tap the calculator or line up the receipts on the floor. My body is doing it, even if I don't know why. But, you know, since you mention an outside force... there is something else that kind of feels like an outside presence is involved, just not physically controlling my muscles. 

It's more about what I'm seeing when I'm working. And I know it sounds completely strange, I really do, and I've been kind of afraid to even bring it up because I know how it sounds, but... I get convinced that certain numbers at work are actually messages. Specifically about me. Like, I'll be doing the data entry for accounts payable—which I usually do on Tuesdays and Thursdays because that's when the big vendor batches come in from the mailroom—and I'll be looking at the screen, and suddenly I just *know* that certain invoice totals, specific client account numbers, and even the net-30 due dates aren't just random business data. I get this overwhelming feeling that they are messages directed entirely at me. 

Like last week, there was this invoice from our main office supply vendor, and the total was $412.18, and the due date was the 18th, and the account number ended in 412, and it just... it felt like someone, or some system, was trying to tell me something. I actually got so worked up about it that I took the physical paper invoice into my supervisor's office. His name is Mr. Henderson, and I usually hate interrupting him because he's always on these long conference calls with corporate, but I just had to show him. 

And he was really patient about it, honestly. He pulled up the vendor history on his monitor and went through it with me, line by line. He showed me the purchase orders for the printer toner and the copy paper, and proved to me that the math was completely right and that they were just totally normal, everyday accounting entries. And logically, I saw that. I watched him do the math. But the thing is... even when he shows me that they are normal entries, and even after I go back to my desk, I still can't shake it. I still feel like they are tracking me. Like whoever is sending these numbers is watching me through the system to see whether I understand the pattern they're laying out in the ledgers. So, it's not a force moving my hands, but it definitely feels like some outside force is communicating with me through the bookkeeping, if that makes any sense at all.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient describes a fixed belief that invoice numbers are personal messages and that they are being tracked, which persists even after their supervisor provides logical evidence to the contrary.
symptom_reasoning.S066: The patient mentions engaging in repetitive behaviors like tapping the calculator and lining up receipts on the floor, noting their body does it even if they 'don't know why', which indicates compulsions.

Like, most days, I'll see a text pop up on my phone from my friend Mark—he's always trying to get me to come out to these local music shows or check out these art projects he's working on, things I used to really be into—and I just... I let it sit there. I don't even open it because then he'll see the read receipt. I just leave it unread. 

And it's not that I don't want him to be happy, but I just feel so flat inside, even when he's talking about stuff that used to be fun. I skip hanging out after my night classes at the community college, too. People will be going to grab a slice of pizza or something, and I just walk straight to my car. I just don't have the energy to put on a face, you know? To force myself to smile or sound excited when everything inside just feels like a straight, flat line. So I guess, yeah, people have noticed, but it's not that I don't care. It's just... I don't know how to make myself look or sound like I care anymore.

symptom_reasoning.S024: The patient describes feeling 'so flat inside' and that everything feels like a 'straight, flat line,' indicating emotional numbness.

turns.doctor_question: Do you believe that numbers or account entries are sending messages specifically meant for you?
turns.patient_response:
Well... okay, so earlier I said no about the numbers sending messages, and I know I sounded really sure about that. But... I mean, I guess it's more complicated than just "yes" or "no," right? Because, like I said, I look at numbers all day. Eight hours a day, sometimes nine if it's the end of the month and we're closing the books. And most of the time, yes, they are just numbers. Just data. But... sometimes... 

I know it sounds strange, really strange, especially coming from someone who literally does bookkeeping for a living, but sometimes I get absolutely convinced that certain numbers are... well, they're not just data. Like, specific invoice totals, or the account numbers for certain vendors, or even the net-30 due dates on the accounts payable aging report... I start feeling like they are messages. About me. Specifically meant for me to find. 

Like, last Tuesday, I was reconciling the bank statement against our general ledger, and I noticed this sequence of invoice totals—$412.50, $41.25, and then an account number ending in 4125. And I just stopped. I sat there at my L-shaped desk, staring at my dual monitors, and my heart started racing because I just knew, I *knew*, it was a message. It felt like the system was trying to tell me something, or maybe test me. So I spent, like, three hours digging through old archived files, pulling up vendor histories from like three years ago, trying to trace the origin of the 4125 pattern, completely ignoring the rest of the daily deposits I was supposed to be working on. 

My supervisor, Linda, she came over because she noticed I hadn't submitted the daily reconciliation report yet. She's usually really nice, she's been there for like fifteen years, and she sat down with me and looked at my screen. She pulled up the original invoices and the vendor contracts, and she walked me through it, step by step, showing me exactly why those totals were what they were. Like, one was just a standard order of printer toner with sales tax, and another was a prorated software license fee. She showed me all the documentation, proving they were just completely normal, everyday business entries. 

And logically, when she was explaining it, I could hear her words, and I could see the math on the screen. But even after she walked away, even after I finally submitted the report and went back to my turkey sandwich... I still felt it. Deep down. I still felt like those numbers were tracking me. Like whoever or whatever put them there was watching to see if I understood the pattern, to see if I was smart enough to figure out what the 4125 meant. And it's not just that one time, it happens with other numbers, too. It's like I can't shake the feeling that there's a hidden layer of meaning in the spreadsheets that only I am supposed to see, even when Linda proves to me that it's just regular accounting stuff. It's really hard to explain, but it just feels so real when it happens.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient describes a fixed belief that specific numbers and invoice totals are hidden messages meant for them, which persists even after their supervisor provides clear evidence that they are normal accounting entries.

turns.doctor_question: Do you ever feel that someone is watching you or trying to harm you?
turns.patient_response:
Watching me? Like, a person? No, no. I know I just said that thing about the numbers feeling like they were tracking me or testing me, which I guess sounds a little like being watched, but it's not a physical person spying on me or anything like that. And definitely no one is trying to harm me. 

My L-shaped desk is tucked way in the back corner of the accounting floor, and my back is technically to the main walkway, which I guess would make some people paranoid, but I never feel like someone is standing behind me staring at the back of my head. I mean, the only people who even walk by are Dave, who is way too busy stressing out and clicking his retractable pen to care about what I'm doing, and Linda, and she's practically the nicest person in the world. She brings in glazed donuts every other Friday from this little bakery near her house. She's definitely not out to get me or sabotage my work. Nobody is trying to poison my turkey sandwich in the breakroom fridge or anything crazy like that. 

And outside of work, it's the same thing. Like when I'm walking to my car after my night classes at the community college, it's usually pretty dark out by then, especially in the winter, but I don't get spooked. I just walk straight to my car, get in, and drive home. I don't ever look in my rearview mirror and feel like there's someone following my car, and I don't think anyone is hiding in the bushes waiting to jump out at me. I don't feel in danger at all. I'm just a twenty-two-year-old bookkeeping clerk, you know? I don't think I'm important enough for anyone to want to follow me around or hurt me. It's really just that weird hidden-message feeling I get with the spreadsheets sometimes, but not actual people out to get me.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient confirms referential delusions (feeling that numbers in spreadsheets contain hidden messages tracking or testing them) while explicitly denying persecutory delusions (being watched, followed, or harmed by others).

turns.doctor_question: Do you ever hear voices when no one else is around?
turns.patient_response:
Voices? Um... well, I mean... yes. But it's not like a whole crowd of people yelling or anything like that. It's usually just this one specific voice, and it only really happens when I'm completely by myself. 

Like, I'll be sitting at my desk—that L-shaped one I was telling you about, tucked away in the back corner of the accounting floor. It gets really quiet back there, especially around four-thirty when Dave is off getting his afternoon coffee and Linda is wrapping up her daily emails. I'll just be sitting there, staring at my dual monitors, maybe scrolling through a massive Excel spreadsheet for the month-end reconciliation, and out of nowhere, I'll hear this man's voice. And it sounds so incredibly real, like someone is leaning right over my shoulder. He'll say something really specific, like, "check line seven." 

And I mean, it's so clear and loud that I physically turn my office chair around. I'll spin around expecting to see Dave standing there holding his mug, or maybe a courier who wandered into the wrong department, but... there's literally no one. Just the empty carpeted walkway and the hum of the overhead air conditioner. I'll even stand up and look over the cubicle wall just to be absolutely sure, but I'm completely alone. 

And it's not just at work, either. It happens sometimes when I'm leaving my night classes at the community college, too. Like I said before, I usually just walk straight to my car, and it's pretty dark and empty out in that parking lot by the time my accounting ethics class gets out. Sometimes, when I'm halfway across the asphalt, just me and the orange streetlights, I'll hear that exact same man's voice. He'll say something like, "you missed the sign." 

I'll stop dead in my tracks right there in the cold. I'll look all around, checking behind the parked cars, looking back toward the brick wall of the science building, because I swear to you, it sounds like a real person is walking two steps behind me. But the lot is totally empty. And then I just stand there overthinking it, wondering, what sign? Did I miss a literal parking sign, or does he mean a sign like the weird number patterns at work? It really messes with my head because the voice doesn't feel like a thought inside my brain, you know? It sounds like it's traveling through the air, hitting my eardrums exactly the way your voice is right now. I've even pulled my phone out of my jacket pocket to see if maybe a YouTube video started playing by accident, or if I pocket-dialed a podcast, but my screen is always black. It's just... it's just this guy's voice speaking right to me, and I have absolutely no idea where it's coming from.

symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient explicitly confirms hearing a man's voice speaking to them when they are completely alone, describing it as sounding like a real person and not just a thought.
